// Code generated by roost servicerpc. DO NOT EDIT.
//
// Generated from the Shop interface in this package. The interface is
// the single source of truth: the wire types, the handler table and the client
// are all derived from it, so a method added to the interface cannot be
// forgotten in the transport — the failure this generator exists to make
// impossible rather than merely detectable.
//
// This file is the transport half and depends on roost-core only. The
// assembly half — Server, OwnerCapabilities, ClientMod, which need
// roost-kit/mods for the Mod and capability names — is shop_rpc_assembly_gen.go
// beside it. The split is what lets an interface move into a core domain
// package and take its wire types, handler table and BusClient along (M-10).
//
// Regenerate with:
//
//	go run github.com/tjbdwanghaibo/roost-codegen/cmd/servicerpc -dir .

package shop

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"time"

	"github.com/tjbdwanghaibo/roost-core/app"
	"github.com/tjbdwanghaibo/roost-core/bus"
	"github.com/tjbdwanghaibo/roost-core/servicerpc"
)

// ServiceType is the bus service type Shop answers on. The client and
// the handlers key on it, so it is one constant rather than a string in two
// places.
const ServiceType = "shop"

// The RPC method names, prefixed with the service type so a bus subject is
// unambiguous when several services register handlers on one connection.
const (
	MethodBuy    = "shop.Buy"
	MethodBrowse = "shop.Browse"
	MethodCancel = "shop.Cancel"
	MethodTouch  = "shop.Touch"
)

// Methods is every method on Shop, in interface order.
//
// RegisterHandlers iterates it, so a method with no handler fails at startup
// with a name rather than at the first call from another process.
var Methods = []string{
	MethodBuy,
	MethodBrowse,
	MethodCancel,
	MethodTouch,
}

// rpcStatus is the envelope every response embeds.
//
// A business failure travels inside the envelope with this package's error
// code; a bus error means the call did not happen. A caller retrying the
// second and not the first is the difference between recovering and
// double-applying, which is why the two are never the same channel.
type rpcStatus struct {
	Code   int32  `json:"code"`
	Reason string `json:"reason,omitempty"`
}

// StatusCode implements servicerpc.ResponseStatusProvider. The methods are
// exported even though the type is not, which is what the assertion in
// servicerpc.CheckResponse needs.
func (s rpcStatus) StatusCode() int32 { return s.Code }

// StatusReason implements servicerpc.ResponseStatusProvider.
func (s rpcStatus) StatusReason() string { return s.Reason }

// statusOf renders an error using this package's Error, so a code that reaches
// a client is the same code a local caller reads off the error.
func statusOf(err error) rpcStatus {
	code, reason := Error(err)
	return rpcStatus{Code: code, Reason: reason}
}

// --- wire types ---

// rpcBuyRequest is the Buy request on the wire.
//
// Its fields are named after the interface method's PARAMETERS, so a payload
// says what the method says. The client takes those parameters as arguments,
// which is what keeps a caller's identity something the compiler asks for
// rather than a struct field whose zero value looks valid.
type rpcBuyRequest struct {
	PlayerID int64      `json:"player_id"`
	Req      BuyRequest `json:"req"`
}

// rpcBuyResponse is the Buy response on the wire.
type rpcBuyResponse struct {
	rpcStatus
	Receipt Receipt `json:"receipt"`
}

// rpcBrowseRequest is the Browse request on the wire.
//
// Its fields are named after the interface method's PARAMETERS, so a payload
// says what the method says. The client takes those parameters as arguments,
// which is what keeps a caller's identity something the compiler asks for
// rather than a struct field whose zero value looks valid.
type rpcBrowseRequest struct {
	ShelfID string `json:"shelf_id"`
	Limit   int    `json:"limit"`
}

// rpcBrowseResponse is the Browse response on the wire.
type rpcBrowseResponse struct {
	rpcStatus
	Page Page `json:"page"`
}

// rpcCancelRequest is the Cancel request on the wire.
//
// Its fields are named after the interface method's PARAMETERS, so a payload
// says what the method says. The client takes those parameters as arguments,
// which is what keeps a caller's identity something the compiler asks for
// rather than a struct field whose zero value looks valid.
type rpcCancelRequest struct {
	PlayerID int64  `json:"player_id"`
	OrderID  string `json:"order_id"`

// rpcCancelResponse is the Cancel response on the wire.
type rpcCancelResponse struct {
	rpcStatus
	Cancelled bool `json:"cancelled"`
}

// rpcTouchRequest is the Touch request on the wire.

// Its fields are named after the interface method's PARAMETERS, so a payload

// rather than a struct field whose zero value looks valid.
type rpcTouchRequest struct {
	PlayerID int64 `json:"player_id"`
}

// rpcTouchResponse is the Touch response on the wire.
type rpcTouchResponse struct {
	rpcStatus
}

// --- server ---

// RegisterHandlers publishes Shop on a bus.
//
// It is called by the process that OWNS the service. The handlers decode and
// call the local implementation and contain no logic of their own: a check
// that lived here rather than in the service would apply only to remote
// callers, and a local caller would bypass it.
func RegisterHandlers(b bus.IBus, service Shop) error {
	if b == nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("shop: bus is nil")
	}
	if service == nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("shop: service is nil")
	}
	handlers := map[string]bus.RpcHandlerFunc{
		MethodBuy: func(ctx *bus.RpcContext) (any, error) {
			var wire rpcBuyRequest
			if err := ctx.Decode(&wire); err != nil {
				return rpcBuyResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrRequestInvalid, err))}, nil
			}
			receipt, err := service.Buy(ctx.Context(), wire.PlayerID, wire.Req)
			return rpcBuyResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(err), Receipt: receipt}, nil
		},
		MethodBrowse: func(ctx *bus.RpcContext) (any, error) {
			var wire rpcBrowseRequest
			if err := ctx.Decode(&wire); err != nil {
				return rpcBrowseResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrRequestInvalid, err))}, nil
			}
			page, err := service.Browse(ctx.Context(), wire.ShelfID, wire.Limit)
			return rpcBrowseResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(err), Page: page}, nil
		},
		MethodCancel: func(ctx *bus.RpcContext) (any, error) {
			var wire rpcCancelRequest
			if err := ctx.Decode(&wire); err != nil {
				return rpcCancelResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrRequestInvalid, err))}, nil
			}
			cancelled, err := service.Cancel(ctx.Context(), wire.PlayerID, wire.OrderID)
			return rpcCancelResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(err), Cancelled: cancelled}, nil
		},
		MethodTouch: func(ctx *bus.RpcContext) (any, error) {
			var wire rpcTouchRequest
			if err := ctx.Decode(&wire); err != nil {
				return rpcTouchResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrRequestInvalid, err))}, nil
			}
			err := service.Touch(ctx.Context(), wire.PlayerID)
			return rpcTouchResponse{rpcStatus: statusOf(err)}, nil
		},
	}
	// Registered against Methods rather than by ranging the map, so a method
	// the interface declares and the table misses fails HERE, with a name.
	for _, method := range Methods {
		handler, ok := handlers[method]
		if !ok {
			return fmt.Errorf("shop: no handler for %s", method)
		}
		if err := b.HandleRpc(method, handler); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("shop: register %s: %w", method, err)
		}
	}
	if len(handlers) != len(Methods) {
		return fmt.Errorf("shop: %d handlers for %d methods", len(handlers), len(Methods))
	}
	return nil
}

// --- client ---

// DefaultCallTimeout bounds one RPC. A call with no timeout is a goroutine
// waiting on a process that may never answer.
const DefaultCallTimeout = 3 * time.Second

// BusClient is Shop over a bus, for the processes that do not own this
// service.
//
// Its method signatures are the interface's, identity included: a caller still
// has to say whose identity it is, and the wire types are this type's
// implementation detail.
type BusClient struct {
	rpc *servicerpc.BusClient
}

// NewBusClient builds a client. serviceType empty means ServiceType; timeout
// non-positive means DefaultCallTimeout.
func NewBusClient(b bus.IBus, serviceType string, timeout time.Duration, opts ...servicerpc.Option) (*BusClient, error) {
	if b == nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("shop: bus is nil")
	}
	if serviceType == "" {
		serviceType = ServiceType
	}
	if timeout <= 0 {
		timeout = DefaultCallTimeout
	}
	// At least one method routes by key, so the picker that reads the key is
	// installed here rather than left to each deployment to remember. A
	// caller's own options come after, so it can still override.
	//
	// This matters for a specific reason: a service whose state is partitioned
	// across instances — a queue kept whole in one key, say — has its
	// throughput bounded by contention on that key, and round-robin routing
	// turns that bound into cross-replica contention. Routing by key makes the
	// contention in-process instead. It is the difference between a design
	// cost and a design defect.
	options := append([]servicerpc.Option{
		servicerpc.WithKeyAffinity(servicerpc.AffinityKeyFromContext),
	}, opts...)
	return &BusClient{rpc: servicerpc.NewBusClient(b, serviceType, timeout, options...)}, nil
}

func (c *BusClient) call(ctx context.Context, method string, req any, resp any) error {
	if c == nil || c.rpc == nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("shop: client is not configured")
	}
	return c.rpc.CallChecked(ctx, 0, method, req, resp, "shop call failed")
}

// Buy places an order. Idempotent per RequestID.
// Buy implements Shop.
func (c *BusClient) Buy(ctx context.Context, playerID int64, req BuyRequest) (Receipt, error) {
	var resp rpcBuyResponse
	err := c.call(ctx, MethodBuy, rpcBuyRequest{
		PlayerID: playerID,
		Req:      req,
	}, &resp)
	return resp.Receipt, err
}

// Browse implements Shop.
func (c *BusClient) Browse(ctx context.Context, shelfID string, limit int) (Page, error) {
	// Routed by shelfID: every call carrying the same key reaches the
	// same instance, so contention on that key stays in one process.
	ctx = servicerpc.WithAffinityKey(ctx, shelfID)
	var resp rpcBrowseResponse
	err := c.call(ctx, MethodBrowse, rpcBrowseRequest{
		ShelfID: shelfID,
		Limit:   limit,
	}, &resp)
	return resp.Page, err
}

// Cancel reports whether it cancelled anything.
// Cancel implements Shop.
func (c *BusClient) Cancel(ctx context.Context, playerID int64, orderID string) (bool, error) {
	var resp rpcCancelResponse
	err := c.call(ctx, MethodCancel, rpcCancelRequest{
		PlayerID: playerID,
		OrderID:  orderID,
	}, &resp)
	return resp.Cancelled, err
}

// Touch has no results beyond the error.
// Touch implements Shop.
func (c *BusClient) Touch(ctx context.Context, playerID int64) error {
	var resp rpcTouchResponse
	err := c.call(ctx, MethodTouch, rpcTouchRequest{
		PlayerID: playerID,
	}, &resp)
	return err
}

// --- capability ---

// capability is what a Mod puts in the registry.
//
// It exists because converting to the interface at the registration call site
// does not do what it looks like it does: `Value: Shop(x)` stores an any
// whose dynamic type is still x's — Go does not box an interface inside an
// interface — so an assertion on the concrete type succeeds anyway. Wrapping
// the interface in a struct makes the dynamic type this wrapper, which
// satisfies Shop and nothing else.
//
// The consequence is the one that matters: a consumer cannot bind to the local
// implementation and then break on the day this service moves into its own
// process.
//
// It forwards each method explicitly rather than embedding the interface, and
// that is not style. Embedding names the field after the type, so an interface
// with a method of its own name — Rank.Rank, Match.Match — would have the
// field shadow the method and the wrapper would not satisfy the interface at
// all. The second service this generator ran against had exactly that shape.
type capability struct{ inner Shop }

func (c capability) Buy(ctx context.Context, playerID int64, req BuyRequest) (Receipt, error) {
	return c.inner.Buy(ctx, playerID, req)
}

func (c capability) Browse(ctx context.Context, shelfID string, limit int) (Page, error) {
	return c.inner.Browse(ctx, shelfID, limit)
}

func (c capability) Cancel(ctx context.Context, playerID int64, orderID string) (bool, error) {
	return c.inner.Cancel(ctx, playerID, orderID)
}

func (c capability) Touch(ctx context.Context, playerID int64) error {
	return c.inner.Touch(ctx, playerID)
}

// Capability wraps a Shop for registration. Both Mods use it, so the
// capability's dynamic type is the same whichever process published it.
func Capability(service Shop) Shop { return capability{inner: service} }

// --- capability name ---

// CapabilityName is the registry key both Mods publish under.
//
// It is declared here, from the interface's marker, so the name and the
// transport that depends on it are one fact. A repository that also keeps a
// central table of capability names should assert equality against this
// constant rather than repeat the string — two literals of the same name is
// how a Mod ends up ordered by one and looked up by the other.
const CapabilityName app.ModName = "service.shop"

// LocalCapabilityName is published ONLY by the owning Mod, and it is how a
// process knows it owns this service.
//
// The alternative was to look up CapabilityName and ask whether the value is a
// *BusClient. That does not work, and finding out why is worth recording: the
// capability is deliberately wrapped so its dynamic type satisfies the
// interface and nothing else, which is exactly what defeats the assertion. The
// first version of this generator shipped that check, and the unit test for it
// passed only because it registered an unwrapped client — not what a Mod does.
//
// Asking "is the local implementation published here" is also the question
// that was actually meant. Type-sniffing for one particular remote
// implementation is a proxy for it, and a proxy that a wrapper, a test double
// or a future in-process forwarder each break differently.
const LocalCapabilityName app.ModName = "service.shop.local"

var (
	_ Shop = (*BusClient)(nil)
	_ Shop = capability{}
)
